wu: Two Truths and a Lie: Students write three sentences about their recent experiences using present perfect or past simple. They read them aloud, and classmates guess which is the lie. Teacher models first: 'I have visited the American Space Oujda twice. I went to Marrakech last month. I have never eaten couscous.'
wuAlt: Find Someone Who...: Students mingle to find classmates who have done specific actions (e.g., 'Find someone who has watched a movie in English this week'). They write names and ask 'When did you...?' for past simple follow-ups.
Speed Dating Opinions: Students pair up and discuss 'What is the best place to visit in Morocco?' for 60 seconds, then switch partners. Teacher monitors for comparatives/superlatives.
pres: Show two PET writing models (email and article) on the projector. Highlight paragraphing, opening/closing phrases, and word count. Elicit differences between formal/informal tones. Ask: 'Which is for a friend? Which is for a magazine?' Distribute a handout with PET writing conventions checklist. Check understanding with quick 'True/False' questions (e.g., 'Articles need a title - T/F').
presAlt: Realia Analysis: Bring in printed emails/articles from local magazines (e.g., 'TelQuel' in English). Students in groups circle paragraph breaks and salutations. Teacher elicits why structure matters for PET.
Mentimeter Word Cloud: Students submit words they associate with 'email writing' and 'article writing'. Teacher groups into formal/informal categories and discusses differences.
prac: Guided PET Writing Task: Students choose one prompt (email: 'Write to your friend about a bad experience at a restaurant' or article: 'Write a review of a Moroccan festival'). They draft 80-100 words using a paragraphing template (Introduction, Body, Conclusion). Teacher circulates to check for PET conventions (e.g., 'Did you start with a greeting?').
pracAlt: Sentence Scramble: Students reorder jumbled sentences to form logical paragraphs (e.g., 'Dear Sarah, / I went to the souk yesterday. / It was very busy. / Love, Ali'). They then write their own scrambled paragraph for a partner to solve.

Role-Play Drafting: Students role-play as customer/restaurant manager to email a complaint, then swap roles. They write the email based on their conversation, focusing on politeness phrases (e.g., 'I would like to complain about...').
ls: PET Listening Comprehension: Play a recording of a model PET article being read aloud. Students listen and answer multiple-choice questions (e.g., 'What is the main topic?'). Replay to check answers and discuss how tone affects meaning (e.g., 'Is the writer positive or negative?').
re: Stand Up if True: Teacher reads statements (e.g., 'You have written an email today', 'You like Moroccan festivals'). Students stand if true, sit if false. Fast-paced review of present perfect/past simple.
prod: Peer Review Checklist: Students swap drafts and use a PET writing checklist (e.g., 'Is the word count 80-100?', 'Are there paragraphs?'). They score each other and give one positive comment and one suggestion. Teacher models first: 'Your article has a clear title. You could add more details about the festival.'
rw: Reading for Structure: Students read two short PET articles (e.g., 'Best Places to Study in Oujda', 'How to Prepare for PET'). They underline topic sentences and circle linking words (e.g., 'First', 'However'). Then, they write a 50-word summary of one article using the same structure.
st: Closing Reflection: Teacher says, 'Today we practiced PET writing conventions and paragraphing. Thank you for your hard work. See you next week!'
g: Teams race to write a 3-paragraph email from prompts, first correct team wins points.
Students spot PET writing errors (e.g., missing greeting, no paragraphs) in a sample text.
Students write a 100-word article in 10 minutes, closest to 100 wins.
Students sort phrases (e.g., 'Dear Sir' vs. 'Hey') into email/article categories.
Students pitch their article idea to the class in 30 seconds, best pitch gets a sticker.
diff: Fast finishers / stronger learners: Write a second email/article on a different prompt and add extra details.
Support / weaker learners: Use a sentence starter template (e.g., 'I am writing to... because...') for their draft.
hw: Complete the PET writing task at home (email or article) and bring it next class.
Read a short English article online (e.g., BBC News) and identify 3 linking words and 2 topic sentences.
Write a 50-word review of a Moroccan restaurant or cafe using comparatives (e.g., 'The food is better than...').
tip: Encourage students to share real-life contexts (e.g., writing about local festivals like the Green March) to make PET tasks more meaningful and culturally relevant.
